resources.string: How mesangial cells support the glomerulus
A qualitative close-up of a mesangial cell between capillary loops in a healthy glomerulus. Structures, debris and motion are schematic and not to scale.
The glomerulus is a tuft of small blood vessels. Inside the tuft, mesangial cells and their surrounding matrix occupy the spaces between capillary loops, outside the blood channel.
The mesangium and the filtration wall
At the outer capillary wall, podocyte foot processes rest on the glomerular basement membrane. The mesangial cell sits between loops and is not a layer of the filtration barrier.
Mesangial cell processes connect through the nearby matrix to the capillary walls where the loops meet the mesangium. Those connections help the loops hold their shape as blood flows.
Mesangial cells can take up some large molecules and debris already in the local matrix. Here, a fragment is shown entering a small compartment in the cell rather than passing into the urinary space.

As mesangial tension changes, a nearby capillary loop can become a little narrower or wider, changing how much of its wall is available for filtration. A single mesangial cell does not set the filtration rate of the whole glomerulus.
